text: Then the whole assembly rose and led him off to Pilate.
They began to accuse him, saying, "We found this man subverting our nation. He opposes paying taxes to Caesar and claims to be Christ, a king."
So Pilate asked him, "Are you the king of the Jews?" "You have said so," Jesus answered.
Pilate said to the chief priests and the crowds, "I find no guilt in this man."
But they insisted, "He stirs up the people, teaching all through Judea. He started in Galilee, and he has come all the way here."
When Pilate heard this, he asked whether the man was a Galilean,
and learning that he came under Herod's jurisdiction, he sent him over to Herod, who was also in Jerusalem during those days.
When Herod saw Jesus, he was delighted, for he had wanted to see him for a long time because of what he had heard about him, and he was hoping to see him perform some sign.
He questioned him at length, but Jesus gave him no answer at all.
The chief priests and the scribes stood there, vehemently accusing him.
Then Herod and his soldiers treated him with contempt and mocked him. They dressed him in a splendid robe and sent him back to Pilate.
That very day Herod and Pilate became friends; before this they had been enemies.
Pilate then called together the chief priests, the rulers, and the people,
and said to them, "You brought me this man as one who was misleading the people. I examined him in your presence and found no basis for your charges against him.

versions.text: and said to them, "You brought me this man as one who incites the people to revolt. I examined him in your presence and found no basis for your charges against him.
versions.explanation: ἀποστρέφοντα means 'turning away' or 'misleading'; 'incites the people to revolt' imports a stronger political charge than the verb carries and duplicates the wording of v. 5. 'Misleading' keeps the sense while remaining natural to read aloud.

text: Neither did Herod, for he sent him back to us. Clearly he has done nothing to deserve death.
So I will have him flogged and release him."
(He was obliged to release one prisoner to them at the festival.)[fn: This verse is absent from a number of early manuscripts.]

versions.text: (He was obliged to release one prisoner to them at the festival.)
versions.explanation: This sentence is missing from many early manuscripts. A brief textual footnote would help readers understand why it is set off in parentheses.

text: But they all shouted together, "Away with this man! Release Barabbas to us!"
Barabbas had been thrown into prison for an insurrection in the city and for murder.
Pilate appealed to them again, because he wanted to release Jesus.
But they kept shouting, "Crucify him! Crucify him!"
A third time he said to them, "Why? What evil has this man done? I have found in him no guilt deserving death. So I will have him flogged and release him."
But they pressed him with loud shouts, demanding that he be crucified, and their shouting prevailed.
So Pilate passed sentence, granting their demand.
He released the man who had been thrown into prison for insurrection and murder, the one they asked for, and he handed Jesus over to their will.
As they led him away, they seized Simon, a man from Cyrene who was coming in from the country, and laid the cross on him to carry behind Jesus.
A great crowd of people followed him, including women who were mourning and wailing for him.
Jesus turned to them and said, "Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for me. Weep instead for yourselves and for your children.
For look, the days are coming when they will say, 'Blessed are the barren, the wombs that never bore, and the breasts that never nursed.'

versions.text: For the days are coming when they will say, 'Blessed are the barren, the wombs that never bore, and the breasts that never nursed.'
versions.explanation: The emphatic ἰδού ('look/behold') is dropped. Restoring it preserves the urgency of the prophecy and reads well aloud.

text: Then they will begin to say to the mountains, 'Fall on us!' and to the hills, 'Cover us!'
For if they do this when the wood is green, what will happen when it is dry?"
Two others, both criminals, were also led away with him to be executed.
When they came to the place called The Skull, they crucified him there along with the criminals, one on his right and the other on his left.
Jesus said, "Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing."[fn: Several early manuscripts do not contain this sentence.] And they divided up his clothes by casting lots.

versions.text: Jesus said, "Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing." And they divided up his clothes by casting lots.
versions.explanation: The prayer of forgiveness is absent from several important early manuscripts; a short textual footnote is customary and informative here.

text: The people stood watching, but even the rulers sneered at him, saying, "He saved others; let him save himself, if he is the Christ of God, the Chosen One."

versions.text: The people stood watching, and the rulers sneered at him, saying, "He saved others; let him save himself, if he is the Christ of God, the Chosen One."
versions.explanation: The καί is ascensive ('even the rulers'), contrasting the silently watching people with the mocking leaders; the current rendering loses this contrast.

text: The soldiers also mocked him. They came up and offered him sour wine,
saying, "If you are the king of the Jews, save yourself!"
There was also an inscription above him: "This is the King of the Jews."
One of the criminals hanging there hurled insults at him: "Aren't you the Christ? Save yourself and us!"
But the other rebuked him: "Have you no fear of God, even now that you are under the same sentence?
We are getting what we deserve for what we did, but this man has done nothing wrong."
Then he said, "Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom."
And Jesus said to him, "Truly I tell you, today you will be with me in paradise."
It was now about the sixth hour, and darkness came over the whole land until the ninth hour,[fn: That is, from about noon until about three in the afternoon.]

versions.text: It was now about the sixth hour, and darkness came over the whole land until the ninth hour,
versions.explanation: For oral reading, a footnote clarifying the Jewish reckoning of hours helps listeners grasp the timing without altering the text.

text: for the sun's light failed. And the curtain of the temple was torn in two.
Jesus called out with a loud voice, "Father, into your hands I commit my spirit." And with these words he breathed his last.
When the centurion saw what had happened, he praised God and said, "Surely this man was righteous."
And all the crowds who had gathered for the spectacle, when they saw what had happened, went home beating their breasts.
But all who knew him stood at a distance, along with the women who had followed him from Galilee, watching these things.
Now look, there was a man named Joseph, a member of the council, a good and righteous man,

versions.text: Now there was a man named Joseph, a member of the council, a good and righteous man,
versions.explanation: The attention-marker ἰδού ("behold/look") is dropped. Rendering it keeps the narrative's oral immediacy as Luke introduces a new character.

text: who had not consented to their decision or their action. He came from the Jewish town of Arimathea, and he was waiting for the kingdom of God.
This man went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus.
Then he took it down, wrapped it in a linen cloth, and laid it in a tomb cut in the rock, where no one had yet been laid.

versions.text: Then he took it down, wrapped it in a linen cloth, and laid him in a tomb cut in the rock, where no one had yet been laid.
versions.explanation: The pronoun shifts abruptly from "it" (the body) to "him" within the same sentence, which jars when read aloud. Keeping "it" throughout matches the antecedent "the body of Jesus" and reads smoothly.

text: It was the day of Preparation, and the Sabbath was beginning to dawn.

versions.text: It was the day of Preparation, and the Sabbath was about to begin.
versions.explanation: The Greek ἐπέφωσκεν pictures the Sabbath "dawning" as the evening light came on; "beginning to dawn" preserves that image while remaining clear. A brief footnote explaining that the Jewish day began at sunset could also help hearers.

text: The women who had come with him from Galilee followed and saw the tomb and how his body was laid in it.
Then they went home and prepared spices and ointments. And on the Sabbath they rested, according to the commandment.
